newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - March 19.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - March 19.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- THYSSEN PLEDGES TO FIGHT KRUPP HOSTILE BID

German steel and engineering group Krupp Hoesch has announced a hostile bid for rival industrial company Thyssen, a move that would create one of the world's biggest steelmakers. Hostile takeovers are rare in Germany, and Thyssen is expected to fight vigorously against the offer. About 80 percent of the shares in Thyssen, which is valued at DM13.6 billion (5 billion stg) by the bid, are widely held.
-- BT AND TELEFONICA PLAN STRATEGY LINK-UP

Plans by British Telecom to form a strategic alliance with Telefonica of Spain could force a fundamental realignment of the global telecoms market. Telefonica International (Tisa), the holding company in which BT is considering taking a stake, already has holdings in several South American operators including Argentina, Chile and Peru. By linking with BT, Telefonica may be forced to withdraw its 25 percent stake in the Unisource alliance of smaller European operators. Such a move would be a blow to US telecoms giant AT&T, which had planned to use Unisource as the vehicle for its European ambitions.
-- LABOUR PROMISES A MINISTER FOR JOBS

Senior Labour party officials have confirmed the party will refashion the cabinet to reflect its "different priorities" if it wins the election. One key change will be the creation of a cabinet post of employment minister, working under the education and employment secretary, who will be responsible for all employment issues and "promoting labour market flexibility, in Britain and in negotiation with Europe". Labour would also give cabinet rank to a newly re-named overseas aid portfolio.
-- GEC-ALSTHOM PARTNERS STUDY FUTURE OF VENTURE

Serge Tchuruk, chairman of France's Alcatel Alsthom, has said the company and Britain's GEC have embarked on a "fundamental reflection" on the future of their power engineering and transport equipment joint venture, GEC Alsthom. One proposal is for Alcatel to take control of the venture's power engineering business while GEC takes over the rail, shipbuilding and industrial interests. News of the review was detailed as Alcatel announced its annual results, which saw net income rise slightly above expectations to FFr2.7 billion.
-- KAUFMAN SAYS BBC "AMATEUR" GOVERNORS SHOULD GO

The Commons National Heritage select committee has published its report on "The BBC and the Future of Broadcasting", in which it calls for the corporation to be run by an executive chairman and qualified non-executive directors. The report found the BBC could not be expected to compete against global media groups "if it is in the hands of a group of part-time people nominated for various attributes not connected with broadcasting". Committee chairman Gerald Kaufman also suggested the task of regulating issues of taste and decency in BBC programmes should by carried out by an independent body with the power to impose fines.
-- DUMPING CLAIM MAY PROMPT DUTY ON NORWEGIAN SALMON

A confidential report by European Commission experts has accused Norway of dumping, claiming its fish producers have been selling salmon in the EU at less than the cost of production. The report also says Norwegian producers have been paid unfair state subsidies, causing prices to fall and Scottish salmon growers to lose profits. EU chief trade negotiator Sir Leon Brittan was expected to respond to the report by recommending a 13.7 percent duty on imports of Norwegian salmon.
-- EURO-ZONE WATCHDOG TO LOSE ITS TEETH

Monday's meeting of EU finance ministers approved a French proposal to create a "stability council" to co-ordinate economic policy among countries in the planned single currency zone. But the French plan was significantly watered down at the meeting, with the proposed institution being stripped of any real power. Fellow ministers emphasised that the new "informal grouping" could not become a political counterweight to the future European Central Bank, which will have responsibility - along with all 15 finance ministers - for setting currency policy.
-- PRESSURE ON UTILITIES TO SELL CAPACITY

A report from the cross-party Commons trade and industry committee has suggested the government should consider forcing National Power and PowerGen to sell generating capacity unless there is a significant increase in competition in power generation. The committee said it was not convinced that "sufficiently robust competition exists to guarantee that consumers will obtain the best possible prices". The committee also expressed concern the Offer, the electricity regulator, could not intervene in the conduct of the Electricity Pool.
-- DK GIVES SECOND PROFITS WARNING

Publisher Dorling Kindersley has issued its second profits warning in just over three months, citing difficult conditions in the US book and multi-media market. Shares in Dorling, which publishes distinctive reference books and CD-Roms, fell by 16 percent after the surprise announcement. Analysts now forecast full-year profits of about 10.5 million stg for the group, which last year posted pre-tax profits of 17.4 million stg.
-- ITALY IS FIRST COUNTRY TO ISSUE BONDS IN EUROS

Italy has launched a one-billion-euro (720-million-stg) bond issue denominated in euros, the first time a national government has issued such a bond. The move, which was jointly managed by Paribas and SBC Warburg, represents a stepping up of Italy's drive to be a founding member of the European single currency. The issue was bought up quickly by mostly European investors, and a syndicate official said they expect a flood of other debut euro issues in the next few months.
